analysis.one_liner: Eases Superfund liability rules and pays grants to clean up and redevelop contaminated 'brownfield' sites.
analysis.headline: The bill won bipartisan backing and cleared one House committee 30–21, but a second House committee stalled it with months of repeated delays and it died without ever getting a floor vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have made it easier to redevelop contaminated former industrial sites — 'brownfields' — by shielding buyers, neighboring landowners, small businesses, municipalities, and recyclers from federal Superfund cleanup liability, and by paying communities grants to inventory and clean up these sites. It would also have barred federal environmental enforcement at sites being cleaned under approved state programs, let a state's governor block a site from the federal cleanup priority list, and lowered some water cleanup standards. It cleared the House Energy and Commerce Committee but the Transportation and Infrastructure Committee repeatedly put off its review until the Congress ended, and the House never voted on it.
analysis.who_benefits: Developers and buyers of contaminated land gain liability protection that removes the main deterrent to cleaning up and reusing brownfield sites. Communities near brownfields get federal grants for site assessment and cleanup loans. Small businesses, municipalities, waste haulers, and recyclers that sent ordinary trash or recyclables to sites now on the Superfund list get their liability reduced or erased. States gain authority over cleanups within their borders.

how_it_helps.text: The bill's findings state that fear of environmental liability is the main reason owners and developers avoid redeveloping contaminated sites, and it would shield bona fide buyers, innocent landowners, and owners of neighboring contaminated property from Superfund liability if they did not cause the pollution and meet inquiry and care requirements [S2][S4].

It directs the President to create a brownfields grant program: up to $200,000 per site for inventory and assessment, and up to $1 million to capitalize revolving loan funds for cleanup, available to states, cities, redevelopment agencies, and Indian tribes [S2][S4].
It would eliminate the federal permit requirement for the on-site portion of cleanups handled under state programs, removing a procedural barrier to redevelopment [S2][S3].

The amended version requires cleanup priorities to put first those sites with ongoing human exposure at levels of public health concern, and authorizes health services and education for communities affected by releases [S3].

It caps liability at 10–20% of cleanup costs (or exempts it entirely) for small businesses, taxpayers who sent ordinary household trash or sewage sludge to Superfund landfills, and municipalities that own listed landfills — parties that today can face outsized cleanup bills [S3].
It subjects federal facilities to the same cleanup requirements as private parties, including state standards, and lets the EPA issue enforcement orders against federal agencies [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers would absorb cleanup costs shifted to the Superfund by the new liability exemptions, and residents near state-run cleanups could face weaker cleanup standards than federal law currently requires, since states certify their own programs and some water-quality and drinking-water targets would be relaxed.
analysis.who_pays_short: Taxpayers and neighbors of state-run cleanups

drawbacks.text: The bill lowers the cleanup bar for hazardous substances left on site: remediation would have to meet drinking water Maximum Contaminant Levels instead of the stricter Maximum Contaminant Level Goals, and it removes a requirement to meet Clean Water Act water quality criteria [S2][S3][S4].

It bars the federal government from enforcing Superfund law at any site being handled under a state cleanup program that the state itself certifies is protective, which critics of state-program approaches argue invites inconsistent or weaker cleanups; the amended version added a public-participation requirement and exemptions for sites the Governor asks EPA to handle, federal facilities, and emergencies [S2][S3][S4].

By excusing small businesses, municipalities, waste haulers, and recyclers from Superfund liability and having the Superfund absorb their shares, the bill shifts those cleanup costs onto federal taxpayers [S3].

It lets the President add a site to the National Priorities List only with the Governor's concurrence, giving a single state official power to keep a site off the federal priority list; the committee version carved out exceptions for multi-state releases and cases where the state itself is a major responsible party [S2][S3].

The bill requires a federal study of the cancer potency values of 12 specified hazardous substances, which critics of similar proposals said could delay cleanups pending re-evaluation of known risks [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core bargain is real: liability fear genuinely paralyzes redevelopment of contaminated urban land, and the bill's grants, buyer protections, and relief for small businesses, municipalities, and household-waste contributors would have helped ordinary communities and taxpayers who never caused the pollution. But the bill pays for that partly by weakening cleanup standards and shifting cleanup costs from polluters to the federal Superfund, and by putting state governors and state-certified programs in charge of cleanups that federal law now governs. The committee-amended version added safeguards (public participation, emergency exceptions, exposure-based cleanup priorities), but the drinking-water and water-quality standard rollbacks remained.

outcome.mechanism: It passed the House Energy and Commerce Committee in October 1999 and was formally reported in July 2000, but the House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee, which shared jurisdiction, never finished its review — it granted about twenty extensions stretching from September into mid-December 2000 — and the bill died when the 106th Congress ended on January 3, 2001, without a House vote.

narrative.text: Representative James Greenwood (R-PA) introduced the bill on July 21, 1999 with a bipartisan group of original cosponsors [S1][S4][S5].
A House subcommittee forwarded it to the full Energy and Commerce Committee on a 17–12 vote, and the full committee ordered it reported amended on a 30–21 vote on October 13, 1999 [S6].
The committee formally reported the bill, amended, on July 20, 2000 as H. Rept. 106-775, Part I [S6][S3].

Because the Transportation and Infrastructure Committee also had jurisdiction, the bill needed that committee's action too; it instead granted a series of extensions of its consideration deadline roughly every day or few days from late October through December 15, 2000, and never reported the bill [S6].
The House never voted on the bill, and it expired when the 106th Congress ended on January 3, 2001 [S6][S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The bill's opponents won by default: existing federal Superfund enforcement authority and current cleanup standards stayed intact. Brownfield developers, small businesses and municipalities hoping for liability relief, and communities hoping for federal cleanup grants got nothing from this bill, which died without a vote.

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was bipartisan from day one — 9 Democrats and 7 Republicans joined the Republican sponsor — and the full committee advanced it 30–21, though the record does not show how the committee votes split by party.

industries.industry: Real estate developers and buyers of contaminated land
industries.note: The bill shields bona fide buyers, innocent landowners, and owners of neighboring contaminated parcels from Superfund liability, which its findings say is the main fear blocking brownfield redevelopment. Cleaner, reused urban sites raise surrounding property values and tax bases.

industries.industry: Companies and parties that sent waste to Superfund sites (generators, haulers, recyclers, small businesses, municipalities)
industries.note: The bill caps or erases their cleanup liability and makes the federal Superfund absorb the freed-up shares, shifting costs those parties would otherwise pay onto federal taxpayers.

The bill writes a specific industry-standard site assessment (ASTM E1527 Phase I) into law as the safe harbor for innocent landowners, making commercial environmental assessments a permanent legal requirement in property deals.

Federal enforcement is barred at state-program sites, Governors gain veto power over priority-list additions, and cleanup standards are loosened — but the bill also lets EPA issue enforcement orders against polluting federal facilities and authorizes brownfields grants.

They become eligible for assessment grants and cleanup loan funds, get liability limits on involuntarily acquired or licensed properties, and can settle municipal-landfill liability at 20–35% of costs.
